records.title: Show HN: Kapso – Iterative learning from enterprise data
records.author: alirezamshi
records.storyText:
Hey HN! We're Alireza and Majid building Leeroo (https://leeroo.com/). Previously we’ve built AI systems for products with millions of users, including at LinkedIn and Meta. We’re now focusing on building AI systems for enterprise data. Today, we're open-sourcing Kapso (https://github.com/Leeroo-AI/kapso), an engine that runs experiments, deploys the best solution, and learns from every run.

The nature of data work is iterative: investigate, form hypotheses, experiment, and improve based on what you learn. This bottom-up process is the only way to deliver meaningful outcomes quickly in large, messy enterprise data environments. Consultants gathering context in meetings or teams defining a business ontology upfront to fit into the data has no chance of execution, in quarters and sometimes years. An AI-native system should automate this process, compounding learning to each new investigation and implementation.

For instance, one of our enterprise projects was moving a company off its old data estate onto a lakehouse with more than 30 source-system families, thousands of tables and transformations, and hundreds of BI reports. No individual or AI agent knew how that data estate was connected and operated. The only way to learn it was to investigate the company's repos, dbt models, documentation, and data itself and propose hypotheses about the estate, run experiments, and learn from them, until we understand how each system behaves and under which conditions.

The iterative work goes beyond understanding how data and systems fit together, and the business operations. Building useful software is iterative too. Whether you’re optimizing a warehouse, building a lakehouse pipeline or predicting churn, you need to run experiments and learn what works best in that environment. As you deliver more projects, that know-how compounds, similar in principle to RL. RAGing documentation has little value until it has been tried in a specific environment and the consequences are learned. As with human engineering work, experimentation and learning should happen in a sandbox.

We built Kapso for this kind of work, you give it an objective and success criteria, and it works towards an optimum solution that can be deployed on your stack.

You can view a video walkthrough here: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=W4FHlza1fRs

Here’s how it works…

Kapso has a bank of lessons that are induced or deduced from the past experiments, and each carries a credence score, conditions on where it applies, and the evidence behind it. For each new experiment, an ideation module proposes ideas considering the earlier lessons, re-ranks them by expected return against the budget each would use, and sends the top-ranked ones to the implementor. Because the bank keeps learning from the past experiments in that environment, the proposed ideas are better suited to it than generic hypotheses from an LLM or RAG. Also, results of each experiment are verified by a verifier module that no experiment can access and cheat. As we’ve found when building such systems, sometimes the success criteria and evaluation tests need to be evolved. The experimentation modules can propose updates to the metrics and criteria for the verifier to approve or reject.

After each run, learn() updates the bank of lessons’ scores and boundaries using the evidence from that run. Changes to the bank can also be A/B tested by running otherwise identical builds with the previous and updated banks. The bank is built on git, so you can share your experience with others, list the banks available to you, and update them (`kapso experience share/list/update` in CLI). The system is model-agnostic and coding-agent-agnostic.

kapso.deploy(solution, target_stack) follows the same workflow, runs a shorter experimentation loop to adapt the best solution to the target stack (e.g. Docker, Modal, BentoCloud, LangGraph). Every domain has a harness to start from, you can write your own domain harness with /kapso:harness in the plugin or through CLI (kapso harness new <name>), and compound over that by running experimentations.

We ran it on some public benchmarks and live competitions, with the following results…

- Predictive modelling on relational databases: first on RelBench, Kumo AI (now Nvidia) and Stanford's benchmark, ahead of the best tabular foundation model (https://star-project.stanford.edu/relbench/leaderboard/). This shows that keeping the learning in the harness-level can beat foundational table models. Updating a bank of lessons costs far less than retraining a tabular foundation model.

- ML Engineering: First on OpenAI's MLE-bench at submission, still among the top open-source systems (https://github.com/openai/mle-bench/pull/107).

- AI competitions: ahead of the best agent the ALE-Bench authors at Sakana AI reported, and running autonomously at the live International Olympiad in AI 2026, above all 471 human contestants and in the top three AI systems (https://ioai-official.org/ai-models-track/ioai%c2%b2-2026-re...).

We have a public bank for ML and Data at Leeroopedia (https://leeroopedia.com/): around 100k pages extracted by experimenting on papers and repos, about 6M requests a month, about 28% from AI agents.

If you are at a growing company with a complex data estate across multiple systems and functions, and your data and AI team is stretched, we would love to help!

https://github.com/Leeroo-AI/kapso

records.title: Show HN: Apron Chat Protocol
records.author: shazow
records.storyText:
Hi HN friends - I've been obsessed with chat protocols for ages - one previous project is ssh-chat (https://ssh.chat/)

I come bringing a new kind of chat protocol that I've been working on since I spent quite a lot of time exploring the 14 other competing standards we've come up with in the past few decades.

The protocol details are here: https://apron.chat

I'm hoping that Apron will better reflect our needs beyond 2026, which I expect will move more and more toward semi-private chats rather than global social networks.

Come say hi on the live public demo: https://web.apron.chat

Some fun facts:

- The demo server runs in a Cloudflare Durable Worker. It's quite efficient, since it's hibernated except for when a message comes in. Easy to self-host this in the free tier.

- Despite the JSON protocol being intentionally unabbreviated ("message" instead of "msg", etc), a typical Apron session still uses almost half as much bandwidth and messages compared to an equivalent Matrix or XMTP session. This is largely because Apron minimizes the number of roundtrips and state required for common chat scenarios. Also it compresses very nicely!

- The official reference client is a PWA (Apron Web), we also have a TUI, macOS, and an iOS implementation by third party Apron-enjoyers. There's two reference server implementations (Cloudflare worker in TS and a Go implementation), plus a bunch of minimal implementations.

- My favourite fun capability is embedding streaming messages, great for LLM outputs. This can be done just by piping to a curl command, no additional dependencies. There's also a mode for streaming a terminal (by piping something like `script` from util-linux which handles row/col/baud flushing, no special dependencies either). See section 4.8 for details: https://apron.chat/protocol#48-embeds-and-avatars

records.title: Show HN: RealtimeVAD – trading false positives for 110ms earlier end-of-speech
records.author: koljab
records.storyText:
Hey guys. I recently watched the latency reports for my local voice assistant, which show a waveform plus silero probability for voice activity. I noticed silero lags visibly on the speech off signal.

There had to be a method to get this signal closer to what I felt is optimal. My idea was to use a 10 ms energy detector with a threshold that adapts to environment or room noise. Which worked amazingly well. It created more false positives but in my speculative generation pipeline that would not matter. If it's wrong and the user continues speaking I can abort the pipeline fast.

I benchmarked my solution over ~3200 turns from my assistant logs and it came out ~110 ms faster initially. Still 100 ms now after some a fix which was needed for quiet speech.

I made it public if you want to have a look. If you measure it on your data I really appreciate any feedback. There's a benchmark script in the repo.

Thx for reading, have a good day folks.

records.title: Show HN: Cerulion – ROS 2-compatible robotics runtime with multi-process replay
records.author: lakshays
records.storyText:
Hey HN! I'm Lakshay. Raveen and I have built Cerulion, a ROS2-compatible robotics runtime written in Rust. We've worked hard on lowering IPC transport latencies without making the single process tradeoff or forcing POD message types. These fast multi-process graphs can then be resimmed deterministically, and existing ROS2 nodes/launch files can run unmodified alongside native Cerulion Rust/Python code. Installation and quickstart (with a one-shot prompt for your favorite coding agent) here at the repo README: https://github.com/cerulion-inc/cerulion

I worked on off-road autonomy during my PhD at MIT, and we kept running into inter-process latency in ROS (2 lidars and 6 cameras). Loaned messages need POD types, which nukes standard, vendor-agnostic Image/PointCloud2. We ended up running some hot paths in a brittle single process, which made debugging a nightmare. I'm sure you've seen the heisenbugs ROS-based stacks can produce, with no way to easily reproduce the consumption order or interleaving of callbacks. Valuable data of runtime failures on the robot was hard to use effectively without deterministic reproducibility.

This is what we fix. Cerulion bags record per-input reads and scheduler traces alongside message content in standard MCAPs. cerulion bag play --resim all --verify re-executes node code on the recorded schedule and compares each byte for exact matches or within defined tolerances. Exit 0 is a match, 1 shows the first topic/frame that diverges, 6 shows schedule divergence and --report gives an optional CI verdict. Eligible ROS2 processes can replay deterministically as well.

Here's the data loop:

1. Run: Dependency-ordered level-based DAG scheduler with periodic/data/sync triggers, I/O deadlines, backpressure, and automatic profiling for process partitioning. Each node by default free-runs in its own process while preserving deterministic replay. Live runs pause/resume, and UMWAIT/WFE parks idle consumers on CPUs that support it. Wall-clock reads and runtime thread spawns in user code rejected at compile time by macros.

ROS 2 is supported with rmw_cerulion for Foxy, Humble, Jazzy and Lyrical, that lets you run ROS2 nodes/launch files unmodified in the same graph as native Cerulion nodes. LD_PRELOAD gives ROS2 code shared memory loans through std::vector/std::string. cerulion ros2 attach folds in already-running ROS2 robots, and cerulion ros2 run/launch lets you run existing ROS2 workspaces on Cerulion without any additional setup (with an optional automatic migrate suggested that rewrites C++ publish sites).

2. Move: iceoryx2 shared memory with no serialization, no payload copy and no payload-sized allocation, including for variable-length messages like sensor_msgs/Image and PointCloud2. Round trip latency for a 1MiB sensor_msgs/Image between two processes is 4.08µs p50, with a tight tail of 7.38µs p99 (under 2x p50), with recording on. This is default Cerulion, against 10.95 ms for default ROS 2 Jazzy. Cerulion's p50 and p99 stay flat from 64B to 16 MiB.

3. Capture: With this round-trip latency, there are no tradeoffs, not for process isolation and not for bagging. We can afford always-on or event-based logging. Flashback is our robot dashcam: keeps ~30s of all logs and message contents in memory and saves it automatically on process crashes, topic stalls or declared incidents/manual triggers.

4. Reach: A free account lets you pair robots and desks, letting all your devices find each other with no config, IP addresses or discovery chatter. Pubsub is authenticated and on-demand, with signed grants that the robot verifies offline. We use Iroh to hole-punch or relay over WAN, and mDNS over LAN to transmit data using QUIC. Remote topics mirror into local shared memory, and each device has a single network gateway.

5. Diagnose: cerulion doctor scans for compile/run-time issues (better than Windows Troubleshooter I promise) and suggests fixes. Hindsight is an early access MCP to let agents analyze your bags.

To get started: go to the repo, install Cerulion with the curl one-liner, and paste the prompt in Claude Code/Codex: https://github.com/cerulion-inc/cerulion#quickstart-run-reco.... Or shift your own gears, it's all in the repo that you should star!

The CLI needs a free account, which we use to make device pairing as easy as AirDrop USED to be ;) Everything runs on Linux (x86_64/ARM64), macOS and Android (JNI), with more platforms coming.

We'd love to hear your feedback! If you run ROS 2 on a real robot, point this at your stack and tell us what breaks.

Docs: https://docs.cerulion.com

Site: https://cerulion.com

records.title: Show HN: Langfuse AI Gateway, open source rust gateway to trace every LLM call
records.author: clemo_ra
records.storyText:
Hi HN, this is Max, Marc and Clemens, co-founders of Langfuse, the open source tool for agent & observability & evals (https://github.com/langfuse/langfuse).

It’s been a minute since our last Show HN in August 2023 (https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=37310070) - we’ve been busy building out and serving our tracing & eval pieces over the past years and have been very lucky to build a successful company and open source project around it. Today, we are happy to show the beta of Langfuse AI Gateway: https://github.com/langfuse/langfuse/tree/main/ai-gateway. You may ask, why an AI Gateway as our second product: it’s been one our community’s strongest asks + integration pattern that we’ve seen. We want to offer a scalable, reliable and secure way to solve for the gateway use case in the same way that we’ve done with tracing/evals over the past years. And we’ve recently grown our team with some excellent folks - expect to see more bigger bets from us.

Our observability SDKs currently see the code you instrument. Much of a company's model traffic runs through code that is not or cannot be easily instrumented: coding agents like Pi, Claude Code and Codex, internal tools, scripts etc. Third party gateways are already popular ways to emit traces to Langfuse and we’re happy to now ship one natively.

You change your base URL and your API key. Langfuse AI Gateway forwards the native request with a provider key that does not need to be distributed across the team. Right now, it doesn't translate between APIs, responses are relayed unchanged. This was a conscious decision to ensure stability for gateway users, as translation between e.g. OpenAI responses and Anthropic messages are imperfect and might lead to subtle failures in your agents.

If you pass a traceparent header, the call lands inside your existing Langfuse traces.

You can try by docker composing langfuse up and then on to http://localhost:3000

--

git clone https://github.com/langfuse/langfuse.git

cd langfuse

docker compose up

--

On Cloud, each call becomes a Langfuse generation with tokens, cost, latency and time to first token. Prompts and outputs are recorded if you opt in. If you self-hosted you can also track nothing, not even metadata.

Some details:

- Written in Rust. Stateless, with no database; it talks only to the Langfuse platform and the providers.

- 22MB Docker image. Under 3ms median overhead with tracing on, 1,000+ concurrent streams on 2 vCPUs.

- MIT licensed. Self-host it with Docker Compose or Helm or use our Cloud version.

- Your provider keys and contracts. We don't resell tokens.

What’s next? - Budget caps per key, user, team

- Custom model aliases and fallbacks

- Guardrails

- PII redaction

- SCIM user provisioning

We’ll be around & looking forward to all questions & comments

records.title: Show HN: KittyBrowser, I built a web browser in your terminal
records.author: graiz
records.storyText:
I'm spending more time in the terminal, and with kitty graphics support now in Ghostty and Rex, I thought a real browser in a coding pane might be possible. It is.

kb drives headless Chrome and draws each frame as pixels, so you get the actual page, not a text approximation.

Key features: - Built in Rust, on headless Chrome - Keyboard shortcuts, mouse clicks, scroll, zoom, find, copy - Frames can go through the terminal itself, so it should work over SSH CLI, MCP and an agent skill, so your coding agent drives the same page you're watching

From its own pane, the agent runs things like: > kb https://news.ycombinator.com/

What I learned: the best way to design a CLI for agents is to watch agents use it. Most of the commands exist because an agent got stuck. I ran multiple agent loops where agents would try to use the documentation, get stuck and itterate on the docs.

Note this project needs a terminal with the kitty graphics protocol (Ghostty, kitty, WezTerm, Rex) and Chrome. Tested on macOS; Linux builds but needs testers. Windows PRs welcome.

cargo install --git https://github.com/graiz/kittybrowser kb news.ycombinator.com

MIT licensed. Feedback welcome.

records.title: Show HN: Wonderchat – A Zendesk alternative that doesn't charge per seat
records.author: walkingsunrise
records.storyText:
Hi HN, I’m Vera, co-founder of Wonderchat.

We started as an AI website agent that answers customer questions from a company’s website and docs. Over time, customers kept asking for the rest of the support stack around it, so we built a helpdesk: live chat, a unified inbox for email and SMS, and a help center (coming soon in a couple of weeks).

The pricing and AI native helpdesk experience is the part I most wanted to change. Most helpdesks charge per seat, so every new teammate adds to the bill, and support teams end up rationing logins. We charge one flat price with unlimited seats. You pay only for AI work: the replies and resolutions the agent handles. Human agents replying to tickets don’t cost anything extra.

We've also rebuilt the entire customer service helpdesk around the ideas of AI agent deflecting frontline support tickets first, and having an AI helpdesk agent that helps to draft auto replies to incoming tickets. As the human agent approves its responses and sends them out, the AI helpdesk agent learns about the internal support SOPs to then continually draft better AI responses.

The product is built for users to self-serve their customer service operations set up.

You don’t have to open our dashboard to set it up. Open your site’s code in Claude Code, Cursor or any coding agent and paste:

“Follow https://app.wonderchat.io/llms.txt to add a Wonderchat AI support agent to this site. Train it on [your website], test it with a few real customer questions, and add the chat widget to the shared layout.”

A few technical details:

AI answers come from our own retrieval engine, built for large and messy knowledge bases (we have customers with 10,000+ documents)

You can pick which AI model the agent runs on, so you aren’t locked into one provider

It’s still early. Helpcenter is still a build in progress. You can try it free at https://wonderchat.io/, no credit card needed.

I’d especially like feedback on the product, pricing model, and from anyone who is considering a customer service agent and ticketing software, what made you decide on Zendesk/Intercom? What would make you do the switch?

records.author: asimj1029
records.storyText:
hey everyone!

I read alotttt, and i always wondered what if i could turn my favourite story into a comic, or even an animated film. what if i could keep reading forever? that is how i came up with AxiomStory.

the hardest part was mainly consistency

in text, models forgets facts about your stories

in pictures, models dont keep characters consistent, and giving them reference images every time was tedious.

in videos, the model invents a completely new voice, face background and makes you lose that immersion when you change b/w shots

i've created AxiomStory to fix all of that, its a tool to create consistent stories. it reads your story and builds a wiki of the characters, places, plots etc! it uses that wiki along with other things to find inconsistencies.

The wiki also keeps image and voice references for every character, so text, images and even long ai videos stay consistent.

Hey y'all, I'm Nick. I wanted to share a side project I started sometime last month.

I really enjoy incremental games (like Cookie Clicker, Scritchy Scratchy, etc.) and wondered if I could get a coding agent to build a new one every day that I'd actually want to play.

So I built an incremental game development harness with Claude Code. The first games were pretty rough, but I found that adding a few architectural invariants and automated playtesting around things like pacing and progression made a surprisingly big difference. They're now pretty fun most days.

My partner and I have been playing and talking about the games each day, and after some encouragement from a teammate, I figured I'd share the experiment with the HN community.

The code is available here: https://github.com/nickdirienzo/incremendle

It's AGPL in part because it uses Strudel for music generation. I've also tried to be thoughtful about crediting the artists whose work inspires the games.

Would love to hear what you think of this silly experiment!

records.title: Show HN: AI-drop project – drop traffic fast from misbehaving crawlers (AGPL)
records.author: catab
records.storyText:
Hello!

All started with 4 million requests / day on rocketgit.com (AGPL git hosting). Instead of thousands. Enough is enough!

Presentation (8 pages): https://rocketgit.com/user/catalinux/ai-drop/artefacts/downl...

So, I built AI-drop free-software project (AGPL) to block this kind of crawlers. rocketgit.com has a very restrictive robots.txt (only around 10 pages are allowed). But the crawlers are not respecting it. So, who is not respecting it will be blocked.

Limiting by IP or user-agent is not working anymore. The crawlers are using millions of IPs and it takes days to reuse an IP. And they use fake user-agents.

I am using honeypots to build a list of misbehaving IPs which are streamed to downstream instances. Right now I have around 1.573.000 IPv4 and 6.000 IPv6 misbehaving addresses. I keep them in the list only for 7 days to not block somebody legit. I am watching the traffic on rocketgit.com and the solution is working nicely.

It uses an eBPF program to fast drop the packets.

You can try it easily on your Linux servers:

# Check https://rocketgit.com/user/catalinux/ai-drop/pkg # If your distribution is already there, follow the instructions. # It is the best way to keep you up-to-date.

# Look inside 'ai-drop.spec' or 'debian/control' and install the dependencies. git clone https://rocketgit.com/user/catalinux/ai-drop cd ai-drop ./configure make install # edit /etc/ai-drop.conf # Very important: # set 'interface' (non 'eth' are not supported now) # set 'safe_mode = 0' if you only want to evaluate the product.

Then:

systemctl enable --now ai-drop journalctl -f -u ai-drop

# The list of misbehaving IPs will be streamed from the main server.

# Look at the statistics, especially 'drops': ai-drop dump-stats # Output example: # now=1794482762 ipv4_total=0 ipv6_total=0 total=0 \ # ipv4_adds=0 ipv6_adds=0 adds=0 \ # ipv4_updates=0 ipv6_updates=0 updates=0 \ # ipv4_drops=0 ipv6_drops=0 drops=0 \ # ipv4_real_drops=0 ipv6_real_drops=0 real_drops=0 \ # ipv4_expires=0 ipv6_expires=0 expires=0 \ # ipv4_deletes=0 ipv6_deletes=0 deletes=0 \ # last_load=0 daemon_start=0

Please note that no AI was used to build this software.

Thank you for your time!

Catalin(ux) C.M.T. BOIE

records.title: Show HN: ReadyStack.dev – Bit-for-bit reproducible OSS containers
records.author: readystack
records.storyText:
https://readystack.dev

If you are like me, coding LLMs made open source more important not less. A few months ago I wanted to see how far I could get using minimal LLM cost (local on two 3090s and one subscription) to automate OSS containers with a build recipe that matched bits.

That project ended up as ReadyStack.dev. ReadyStack publishes free Community Edition containers for open-source applications. I designed it to be a low cost image standard that puts provenance as a first order concern.

My goal was to see if I could build in trust with my images in a way nobody else had. Use the build recipe and match bits. Each release's build kit includes everything the build needs: upstream source pinned, the OS packages as .debs, the language dependencies, the base images saved by digest, fixed SOURCE_DATE_EPOCH. BUILD_OFFLINE.sh rebuilds with the network off, so mirrors dropping old packages don't matter, and VERIFY_OFFLINE.sh checks your digest against ours.

We currently have 101 of 101 releases reproducing their published linux/amd64 digest in our clean-room rebuild process, which is just a trust signal, but an important one as we don't have much of, if at all. Certainly, not for free.

For full disclosure, I built a sister project, ce.rodeo, which grades container images from all publishers, including ReadyStack.dev. Yes, it is a conflict of interest to grade my own images. I publish the measuring criteria and I needed a standard of what existed so I had to create a grading system first. Happy to hear suggestions.

I started out to do something for OSS. I designed it to run on a skinny budget and it is doing that. It runs on donations, so far just mine.

The bigger idea is that open-source software should be having its greatest era now that everyone has a DevOps genius at their fingertips. I chose to take a leap and build a platform to be part of that.

Happy to answer questions.

records.title: Show HN: Open-source firmware for 2011 Bowers and Wilkins Zeppelin Air
records.author: fellowmartian
records.storyText:
Just wanted to share something I've built.

It's fully reverse engineered, running on an old 2.4 Linux kernel I found on Nokia HD-1, but with a modern all-Rust userspace. Support Airplay 2 and Snapcast. The Airplay 2 implementation synchronizes with real Apple devices down to 1ms in the multi-room configuration. Spotify support is present, but it doesn't work for me because of librespot key issues.

It utilizes the MIPS co-processor cores I have found on it for audio decoding and crypto. There's no FPU on the ARM nor the MIPS, so all the codecs are reimplemented in fixed-point math and made to fit the very small shared SRAM buffers.

The DSP board firmware is also completely replaced. It fixes all the complaints I had about the original device: no source auto-switching, USB audio would de-enumerate when the speaker went to sleep, volume keys were sending HID events instead of using the proper UAC status interrupt endpoint, etc.

I tried getting 24b USB audio to work, but unfortunately the endpoint buffers on this old AVR32 are too small. The the network audio supports full 44.1/48/24b though.

The Wi-Fi chip is very old, there's no upgrading that, so realtime ALAC on Airplay or PCM/FLAC on Snapcast can be spotty if the connection isn't perfect, but Ethernet works too.

The iPod dock doesn't work, mainly because I can't find my old iPod anywhere to develop against. Send PRs if you have one!

Also partly for vanity and partly for UX I updated the LED colors and FX.

records.title: Show HN: Agent-plan a CLI that automatically commits your agent's plans
records.author: ghmeier
records.storyText:
After spending quite a bit of time using various coding agents and a workflow that uses markdown-based research/plan/handoff documents to hold context across sessions, I kept on running into an this question of how and where to store the generated markdown. The contents are usually useful for posterity and future projects in the same feature area. However, it felt burdensome for myself or reviewers to clutter up diffs with largeish markdown documents. This left me with a mess of uncommitted markdown and a waste of tokens having LLMs collate the documentation.

I figured this was the perfect usecase for a small CLI tool and some hooks that automatically create and sync planning documentation for the team. That's how agent-plan got started. It uses an orphan git branch a worktree checkout and symlinks to keep all the planning files available from any branch. There's a claude and codex plugin that install a couple hooks to sync and commit any edits as they happen.

Myself and my team have been using this for the last month or so, and have found that it really smooths out document-driven development. It's straightforward to hand off plans between people, and easy to reference all the older documentation. It also solves a small (but frequent) papercut I had where I'd have to remember file names to reference them in subsequent chats. Since agent-plan stores everything in consistent formatting with some added frontmatter metadata, it's really easily searchable with plain text search.

I figure lots of teams might have a similar sort of problem and I could save you some time.

records.title: Show HN: Deccy – software engineering as decision management
records.author: nelaggy
records.storyText:
Hi HN,

We built deccy out of frustration from working with coding agents.

Although we love the speed that AI has brought to our work, we also want to have control over what we build. While it's not impossible to keep up with the changes AI makes, it is significantly more difficult when compared to writing code ourselves.

We realised that what we cared about most was not controlling every line of the implementation, but preserving our intent (we especially hated when agents would wrongly guess what we wanted). We iterated through planning and spec-driven methods, but found that both writing our own plans/specifications and reading AI-generated versions was tedious and exhausting.

Eventually, we decided to split the specifications up into the decisions that make them up, and get agents to do the boring work of tracking and bookkeeping. deccy is the first realisation of this idea. We're already working on the next iteration, but we wanted to share the mental model we developed.

There's a long way to go from here, and we'd really love any feedback :)

My latest clock is built mainly from empty drink cartons, plus a few skewers, some paper straws, a piece of string, some nuts as weights, and lots of hot glue. The design of the gears and escapement was AI-assisted: Claude built me interactive browser tools that generate templates and 3D-printable jigs and tools.

I’m happy to answer your questions! And to the commenter who suggested I submit trash clock timekeeping as a talk to 40C3: I did, and it got accepted. CU at Congress, I guess!?

records.title: Show HN: Armin – Modern Anki alternative with prerrequisite graphs
records.author: ansanabria
records.storyText:
okay, so a bit of context. back when i was studying at college, i was trying to optimize my learning process as much as possible, and i ended up discovering Anki and spaced-repetition as a concept. i ended up using Anki for quite a while and it did help me. i loved the concept... but i didn't like the app. it had me conflicted. on one hand, it allowed me to properly review the content from my classes (among other stuff), but on the other it had way too many quirks and complicated ways of handling things that i wasn't a fan of (in particular, the UX leaves a lot to be desired, although it has marginally improved in recent years). i ended up churning from Anki and just abandoning the practice of spaced repetition altogether.

after some time, i ended up reading this article recommended by Justin Skycak https://lelouch.dev/blog/you-are-probably-not-dumb/ . the tldr is that knowledge has prerrequisites, and if you don't have them, you won't fully understand what you are trying to learn in the first place. and that was one of my annoyances with Anki. as i kept reviewing stuff (especially pre-made decks) Anki assumes all knowledge is in the same layer of understanding. it assumes that each flashcard is independent from the others, and that makes it difficult to actually progress while trying to learn a particular topic. Justin Skycak (the guy from Math Academy) ended up implementing spaced-repetition + prerrequisite graphs for math learning, and there i ended up seeing we could extend the concept more generally. one of the things Math Academy made me realize is that if we combine spaced-repetition (i.e. when we should review a card) with prerrequisite graphs (i.e. we keep unlocking new knowledge as we learn the prerrequisites), we can learn things more clearly and in a more structured way.

that's where my "bet" goes. i want something like Anki, but with the option to create a graph of prerrequisites (e.g. you can't learn Y until you properly learn X). that's Armin. among other stuff, i also tried to fix some of the annoyances i had with Anki and make it as intuitive as possible to use. this is a non-exhaustive list of the things i worked on for this app:

- UI polish of the interface. i tried to make it as intuitive as possible.

- MCP server for letting agents read, edit and manage cards and decks. in particular, the MCP server is very useful for creating flashcards from any existing content you have. just point your agent to a resource (e.g. a pdf) and it will take its content and transform it into a deck with flashcards with its prerrequisites graph already created.

- Anki-compatibility with caveats. the app supports bringing your existing Anki decks for most decks out there. however, some decks have custom cards that are not so easy to integrate seamlessly. there are plans to support custom cards in the future, but for now they are not implemented.

- graph view that shows all your flashcards. in here, you can create a graph of prerrequisites and further structure your decks.

- "concept cards". they work more like exercises. you provide the template of an exercise (e.g. how to calculate a derivative) and an agent creates variations of that same type of exercise while changing the details (like the values).

we also have a paid plan for creating way more flashcards and use "concept" cards, but i built the free plan with generous limits so you can test the app without any issue. to be honest, i want the app to be as flexible as possible, and most people will probably only need the free plan. but hey, if you find it too tight, please hit me up and i'll see how i can improve the experience for everyone.

the app is open source and MIT-licensed. you can find it here https://github.com/andy-spike/armin

as for the rest, it is the same you would expect from a spaced-repetition flashcard app. please try it out and tell me what you think of it!
